intro: A text does not explain itself. Readers explain it, and they do so from their own place and time. This unit follows Buddhist readers across two thousand years, from a monk answering a Greek king about a chariot to a Dalit leader in 1956 and a Vietnamese monk writing about a cloud in a sheet of paper.

The first chapter traces the teaching of not-self through the classical thinkers: the Pali suttas and the Questions of King Milinda, Buddhaghosa, Nagarjuna and the doctrine of emptiness, Yogacara, and the schools of Tibet and China. The second follows modern readers: reformers, engaged Buddhists, converts and heritage communities, scientists, women seeking ordination and environmentalists.

By the end you will be able to explain how one term, such as not-self, has been read in several ways; describe modern movements accurately and without ranking them; and analyze any reading by asking which passages it cites, what question it answers and which community it speaks for.
bigQuestion: Why do faithful readers of the same Buddhist texts reach such different understandings, and how can a student describe them fairly?

timeline.t: King Menander (Milinda) reigns; the Milindapanha later records his talks with Nagasena
Nagarjuna writes the Root Verses on the Middle Way (dates uncertain)
Asanga and Vasubandhu shape the Yogacara school
Buddhaghosa writes the Visuddhimagga in Sri Lanka
Zhiyi founds the Tiantai school in China
Tsongkhapa founds the Gelug school in Tibet
Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku speak at the World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago
B.R. Ambedkar leads a mass conversion to Buddhism at Nagpur
Thich Quang Duc's protest in Saigon
Thich Nhat Hanh founds the Order of Interbeing
The Dalai Lama's first Mind and Life dialogue with scientists
Sri Lankan women receive full ordination at Sarnath with Korean nuns

words.d: not-self: no aggregate is a lasting self
the five parts of a person: form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness
the argument that 'person' is a name for assembled parts
own-nature: independent essence, which Madhyamaka denies
emptiness: the lack of own-nature in all things
the school that analyzes experience as the work of consciousness
the Huayan idea that each thing reflects every other
movements stressing reason, ethics and science since the 1800s
a name many followers use for Ambedkar's Buddhism
practice that responds to social suffering

test.q: Which sutta argues that no aggregate is self?
Who uses the chariot image in SN 5.10, before the Milindapanha?
test.why: Vajira answers Mara with the chariot image.

test.q: What image does Nagasena use for rebirth without a self?
choices: A flame lit from lamp to lamp
test.why: The lamp shows continuity without identity.

test.q: Which book is Buddhaghosa's summary of Theravada teaching?
test.why: The Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification.

test.q: What did the Abhidhamma schools say each dhamma has?
In MMK 24.18, what does Nagarjuna identify with emptiness?

choices: How things appear and are named in ordinary life
test.why: Conventional truth is the level of everyday names and causes.

test.q: Which Tibetan school did Tsongkhapa found?
Which Chinese school taught the interpenetration of all things?
test.why: Huayan, based on the Avatamsaka Sutra.

test.q: Who led the 1956 conversion at Nagpur?
test.why: Ambedkar led the refuges and his twenty-two vows.

test.q: Which word did Thich Nhat Hanh use for the dependence of all things?
What was Thich Quang Duc's 1963 act a protest against?
choices: Government treatment of Buddhists in South Vietnam
test.why: He protested Diem's policies toward Buddhists.

test.q: Which claim did the Dalai Lama say science allows Buddhists to set aside?
test.why: He applied his principle to the old cosmology.

test.q: What eight rules does the Vinaya say were given for nuns?
test.why: The garudhammas are the eight special rules.

test.q: Which is the fairest way to compare modern readings?
choices: Ask what they cite, what question they answer and whom they speak for

write.prompt: Choose one term, anatta or shunyata, and trace how three readers from this unit understood it. Cite a text for each (for example SN 22.59, the Milindapanha's chariot, MMK 24.18, or a modern writer), explain each reading, and argue why they differ.
tips: Name each text with its section and translation, and mark paraphrases.
Attribute every belief to a reader or school, never to 'Buddhism' as a whole.
Explain differences by the question each reader was answering.
Compare readings; do not declare one correct.
